title: BalancerPoolerV2.migrateMint lacks nonReentrant; ERC1155 receiver callback fires inside a loop that has already mutated NFTMinterV2 state
description:
migrateMint() is `external` with no `nonReentrant`, no `whenNotPaused`, and no caller restriction beyond the implicit ERC1155 balance check. Its body executes a single NFTMinterV2.burn followed by an `amount`-bounded loop of NFTMinterV2.mintFor(NEW_NFT_INDEX, mintRecipient). Each mintFor reaches into OZ ERC1155 `_mint`, which calls `_doSafeTransferAcceptanceCheck(mintRecipient)`. If `mintRecipient` is a contract, control transfers to its `onERC1155Received` between iterations. At that callback boundary, the caller has fully observable, partially-mutated cross-contract state: NFTMinterV2 has already (a) burned `amount` of OLD_NFT_ID from `msg.sender`, and (b) minted `i+1` of NEW_NFT_INDEX to `mintRecipient` while still owing the remaining `amount - (i+1)` mints in the same outer call. mintRecipient is also the caller-controlled recipient — an attacker calling `migrateMint` from their own id-4 holdings can make `mintRecipient` an arbitrary attacker-controlled contract.

The contract is currently exploit-free because (1) `INFTMinterV2(minter).burn(msg.sender, OLD_NFT_ID, amount)` only burns NFTs owned by msg.sender (no force-burn of a third party), (2) the dispatcher's `dispatch`/`pool` paths are already `nonReentrant`+`onlyMinter`, so a callback cannot drive sUSDS/BPT through the same dispatcher, and (3) mintFor itself does not depend on any cross-call reentrancy-sensitive state. However, the pattern is fragile in two specific ways worth fixing:

  (a) If a future story adds any storage to BalancerPoolerV2 that is read post-loop (e.g., an `if (someCounter)` guard, or a per-recipient idempotency map keyed on `mintRecipient`), the receiver callback can mutate that state between iterations because nothing prevents the callback from calling a re-entrant function on the dispatcher that mutates its own storage. Adding the storage later is a likely follow-on (migration counters, migration caps, per-user limits).

  (b) NFTMinterV2's authorizedBurner / authorizedMinter allow-list means the dispatcher holds two pieces of system authority simultaneously inside the loop. Any future authorized-burner adjacent to the loop (e.g., owner adds a second authorized burner that consults NFTMinterV2 totalSupply) reads inconsistent state inside the receiver callback because `_mint` has fired but the dispatcher has not yet completed the migration batch.

Defensive-programming standard says external calls into untrusted contracts (mintRecipient is caller-controlled and may be a contract) inside a loop should be wrapped in `nonReentrant`. ATokenDispatcherV2 already inherits OZ ReentrancyGuard so the modifier is free to apply.
exploit_path:
1. Attacker `A` holds N id-4 NFTs (legitimately bought on secondary market or accumulated via paid mint when id-4 was live).
2. `A` deploys a malicious contract `R` that implements `onERC1155Received` to do work between mint iterations.
3. `A` calls `BalancerPoolerV2.migrateMint(N, address(R))`.
4. NFTMinterV2.burn fires once, removing N id-4 from `A`. The loop begins. On the first iteration, NFTMinterV2.mintFor(6, R) hits ERC1155 _mint, which calls R.onERC1155Received.
5. Inside the callback, R holds 1 id-6 NFT. R is free to: (i) immediately transfer that id-6 to a different address (front-running the rest of the loop), (ii) call view functions on NFTMinterV2 to observe inconsistent state (totalSupply of id-4 dropped by N, totalSupply of id-6 has only increased by 1 of N expected), (iii) call any non-reentrant-guarded function on any other contract that reads NFTMinterV2.balanceOf, ERC1155Supply.totalSupply, or BalancerPoolerV2 storage.
6. Today none of (i)-(iii) gives R anything beyond what it would get if the loop completed first. But the moment any consumer contract (an off-chain reward-claim contract, a Balancer-based phUSD pool that reads totalSupply, a future migration cap on the dispatcher) wires in a balance/supply read, this becomes an exploitable observation window.

No concrete on-chain exploit exists at HEAD. This is a defensive-programming gap that creates a foreseeable hazard the next time the dispatcher or its peers add state that depends on consistent during-migration reads.
mainnet_realism_check: Pure on-chain reasoning. ERC1155 _mint always calls onERC1155Received when the recipient is a contract (OZ implementation, mainnet-correct). The receiver callback boundary inside an N-iteration loop is real and observable.
recommendation: Add `nonReentrant` to migrateMint (ATokenDispatcherV2 already inherits OZ ReentrancyGuard, so the modifier composes for free). Optionally also add `whenNotPaused` if pause-bypass is not intentional (see RAW-005). At minimum, document the deliberate decision to leave the function reentrancy-unguarded so future contributors do not introduce a counter or cap that breaks under the receiver-callback observation window.
